claim: Peirce and Hanson describe abduction as proposing a hypothesis worth testing, not accepting it; deduction then draws consequences and induction scores them. The generate-then-test cycle is the classic frame, and no mechanical rule outputs good hypotheses (discovery-machine objection). Secondhand via SEP only.
agent_test: Check that the scaffold never lets a generated hypothesis count as accepted until code has run it (already G3, G5); log how often S3 output is rejected at S4.

claim: A generate-then-test loop whose test is run by code (program execution, symbolic interpreter) beats direct prompting: ARC 17% direct to 30% with LLM-summarised hypotheses and 33% with human selection (GPT-4, 100 tasks); ACRE raw 64.0 to 82.5 and task accuracy 28 to 59 (GPT-4). But it is not universal: on MiniARC raw accuracy refinement scored 18.7 vs 33.1 for plain input-output prompting. Gap search: in Hypothesis Search the pool held a correct hypothesis in 49 of 100 tasks and 33 became correct programs with a human choosing (d01); Li et al. get an ensemble gain (26.50 vs 18.78 induction, 15.25 transduction) by gating on whether any hypothesis fits the examples (d05).
agent_test: Per problem class, run plain vs hypothesis-then-code-test at equal tokens; keep the loop only for classes where plain pass rate is mid-range, per G12 and G7.

claim: When the model must apply its own proposed rule instead of a code interpreter, the gain mostly disappears: ACRE self-refine with LM interpreter 70.0 raw / 32 task vs 82.5 / 59 with symbolic interpreter; MiniSCAN task accuracy from above 80% to near zero. Voting over samples without a check barely moves (ACRE 64.0 to 65.0).
agent_test: Ablation: S4 with code runner vs the model grading its own hypothesis, same candidates, equal tokens. Expected: code runner wins; this tests G1/G5 directly.

claim: Choosing among given explanations is near human level on short commonsense items but not on long or open tasks: ART human 91.4 vs best 2019 model 68.9; GPT-5.4 87.2 on ART, 88.0 on e-CARE; True Detective best 42.9 vs human average 47; MuSR murder best 68.0 vs human 92.1. Producing explanations open-endedly is much weaker (ProofWriter abductive 21.5% accuracy, diagnosis hit@3 63 vs 98.7 when ranking given options).
agent_test: Measure the gap on our own tasks: give the agent a candidate list vs ask it to generate. If generation is the weak half, spend tokens on S3 diversity and S7 code selection, not on a better judge.

claim: On long detective puzzles the missing piece is the reasoning chain, not the final choice: GPT-4 27% vanilla, 38% chain of thought, 83% when handed the author's golden chain (random 24%, human average 47%).
agent_test: Test whether a retrieved or code-extracted fact table (S2) lifts accuracy in the same way as a golden chain at equal tokens.

claim: LLM abduction degrades fast as the number of required hypotheses or interacting causes grows: InAbHyD multi-hypothesis accuracy from above 80% at tree height 1 to below 50% at height 2 for every model except GPT-4o (true hypotheses 3.0 to 3.5); rule-change attribution 0.90 (no change), 0.32 (one), 0.15 (two or more), 0.03 for interacting changes; GEAR: 70B-class models give about 20% consistent hypotheses.
agent_test: Build a ladder of hidden-cause tasks with 1, 2, 3 interacting causes; check that S6 impasse operators keep accuracy above plain at equal tokens when causes interact.

claim: Strong deduction does not predict strong abduction. Pooled published experiments: median accuracy deduction 79.96%, abduction 42.50%, induction 28.8%. Same syllogism content turned into abduction: GPT-4 41.67% vs 72.22% for deduction.
agent_test: Do not infer abduction skill from deduction benchmarks; include an abduction item class in our bench. The survey median pools mixed datasets and methods, so treat it as a rough ordering only.

claim: Models almost never say no explanation fits (the bad-lot case): GPT-4 chose 'Neither' 0.00% zero-shot in the syllogism abduction task, fallback trivial hypotheses that restate the observation are a common failure in InAbHyD, and on AbstentionBench (20 frontier models, over 35,000 unanswerable questions) reasoning fine-tuning lowers abstention recall by 24% on average and a larger reasoning budget generally lowers it further. DNR Bench shows an explicit instruction can rescue some models (unanswerable items: GPT-4o 0.42 to 0.98, Claude-3.7-Thinking 0.12 to 0.82) but not others (o3-mini-high 0.00 to 0.02, DeepSeek-R1 0.00 to 0.20). None of these tests a candidate pool that lacks the true explanation.
agent_test: Insert a distractor-only candidate set; measure whether S7 with a code-checked good-enough threshold flags the bad lot, versus the plain model. G6 says do not abstain on first pass; this is about flagging, not refusing.

claim: Few-shot demonstrations help abduction only when matched to the test: InAbHyD in-distribution demos raised strong accuracy at heights 3 and 4, height-1-only demos gave no gain; in syllogism abduction few-shot hurt GPT-4 (41.7 to 28.7) but moved Llama-3-70B to 75.5 with 63% on Neither.
agent_test: Demo effects on abduction are unstable across models: avoid fixed few-shot exemplars in S3 unless tested per class and model.

claim: LLMs explain but often do not pick the simplest explanation set: a persistent gap between weak accuracy (explains) and strong accuracy (explains and is simplest), reduced but not closed by reasoning models and buffer-of-thought; fine-tuning on synthetic data raised strong accuracy (Qwen3-4B +11.0 at height 1).
agent_test: Add a code-computed parsimony score (count of hypotheses not needed to cover observations) in S7 and compare to the model's own choice.

claim: Code-computed virtue features beat an LLM judge at picking the better explanation, but only some virtues work: IBE-Eval reaches up to 77% (about 27 points above random, +17.5 over a GPT-3.5 judge on average), Spearman with human choice 0.64 vs 0.31. Consistency is nearly useless (models write consistent stories for wrong options); parsimony beats it by 14 points on average; hedging language was the strongest single predictor. Gap search: no test with modern models or harder tasks was found. Nearest data: a model judge (USC) ties plain voting and sits 6 points (GSM8K) to 20 points (MATH) under the oracle pick (d10); an execution-based agreement score (CodeT) lifts HumanEval pass@1 from 47.0 to 65.8 (d11).
agent_test: On candidate pools with ground truth, ablate each virtue (parsimony, scope, hedging, consistency) as a code score and compare to vote and to a blind judge at equal tokens.

claim: Gold-answer scoring hides underdetermination: about 80% of equally plausible hypotheses were labelled incorrect, and only 35% of 50,340 hypotheses were consistent with the observations. Set-level code scores (consistency, generalisation, diversity) can be computed with no labels, and more diverse sets were more likely to predict hidden cases (odds ratio above 1 in most cells). Label-free preference training gave small gains on 7B models.
agent_test: In S7, group candidates by behaviour on fresh inputs (already in schema) and test whether diversity-aware top-k beats first-passing at equal tokens.

claim: Humans prefer the simpler (fewer-cause) explanation more than probability alone justifies, but weigh both: 96% chose one-cause with no base rates (N=48), 92% chose the more probable disease with base rates; over 144 participants 71% chose simple overall and over a third still did when the complex story was 10 times more likely; with experienced frequencies 41% chose simple at 1:10 (N=108). The effect shrinks when the complex story's joint probability is shown directly (17% simple, N=48). One lab only. Outside-lab tests exist only as moderators, not as replications of these experiments (see K33).
agent_test: Do not assume simplicity is wrong or right; calibrate a simplicity weight on our own ground-truth pools and compare against a fixed prior.

claim: The strength of the simplicity preference depends on causal structure and on how probability is stated: strongest for one cause explaining two independent effects, modest for jointly sufficient causes, reversed in some structures (N=544, abstract only); wording 'most likely' vs 'most satisfying' moves the choice (46% vs 17% simple).
agent_test: Treat any virtue weight as task-structure dependent; restate whether the task asks for likeliest or most satisfying explanation.

claim: Asking people to explain pushes them toward simple, broad hypotheses (five-year-olds prompted to explain chose the common-cause hypothesis more; adults found a 100% rule more often than every control group). Whether this is good depends on the world being simple. LLM follow-up in K27.
agent_test: Self-explanation in S2 may bias toward one unifying rule; test with tasks where the true rule is a two-part exception.

claim: People's credence updates are predicted better by Bayes plus their own explanatory-goodness ratings than by Bayes alone (R2 0.90 vs 0.83, AIC gap above 120, N=26, one urn study reanalysed from Schupbach 2011). A later claim that explanation-weighting people were more accurate is known only from SEP. Douven and Schupbach (2015, Cognition) report three experiments supporting the explanationist view; only the abstract was read (d26) and no outside replication was found.
agent_test: Descriptive only; small sample. No direct agent use; do not copy this as a design rule.

claim: Explanationist updates reach high credence in the truth faster than Bayes in simulations, but the normative case is contested: Pettigrew shows a dumb rule that waits 10 draws scores equal or better on the speed metric; Trpin and Pellert find IBE** reaches Pr(true)>0.95 in about 49-52% of runs vs 11-16% for Jeffrey updating, yet at the first update step it puts above 0.95 on a false coin in 47% of runs vs 3%; Dellsen and Trpin find results depend on task risk and difficulty; Climenhaga and Cabrera (snippets only) argue incoherence and virtues lacking confirmation. Gap search: full text of Trpin and Pellert confirms 47% vs 3% (above 0.95 on a false coin at the first assignment) and 37% vs 1% above 0.99, with the bonus fixed at 0.1 and no test of other sizes (d19). See K26 for the bonus size.
agent_test: Simulation test: bonus-for-best-explanation updates vs plain likelihood weighting over candidate rules, measuring speed to the right rule and rate of early commitment to a wrong one, at equal tokens.

claim: Standard IBE is two stages (generate, pick the best); Dellsen argues for a third consolidation stage and replaces best with a good-enough working hypothesis. The bad-lot problem (best of a poor set) is unresolved; Lipton's catch-all was called uninformative. Philosophical, no measured result.
agent_test: Add a code-checked good-enough gate: adopt only if the best candidate passes an unfitted test; otherwise return to S3 with untried directions.

claim: Deduction-style scaffolds (CoT, ToT, GoT) fail on open abductive diagnosis for four reasons (fabricated evidence, context drift, failed backtracking, early stopping); a state-machine agent with a confidence-gap threshold got Match 39.86% vs about 26% for the best baseline on medical diagnosis, at lower cost ($0.12 vs $0.73 per case). Small multi-role agents (Theorem-of-Thought) gained on 7B models but self-consistency beat them in some cases.
agent_test: Compare a code-driven state machine with an evidence-confidence gate against plain sampling on a diagnosis-style task at equal cost.

claim: Abduction as retrieval or event-cause search can help in applied pipelines: LLM-proposed causes plus search plus a learned scorer improved event rank (GDELT about 40 to about 20; ICEWS about 90 to about 20); abductive RAG HotpotQA F1 75.3 vs 67.8 for plain RAG. Weakly documented, system-specific.
agent_test: Treat as weak lead only; not a basis for an operator.

claim: Whether token-completion LLMs perform abduction at all is contested: Floridi et al. argue they do not (no measured results); Out-of-Context Abduction found GPT-4o picked the right persona in one of three cases (84% vs prior 49%) and not for GPT-4o mini; Pareschi's anecdotes have no baseline.
agent_test: Irrelevant to engineering: judge by checked output (G10), not by whether the process is abduction.

claim: Models need structural hints to attribute rule changes: weaker models score near zero on exact attribution without strong prompt scaffolding, and extra reasoning did not rescue interacting changes. One study.
agent_test: Test whether a code-built table of what changed (S2) restores attribution accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: In sampled hypothesis or answer pools the correct item is often present but not chosen. MATH Llama-3-8B: coverage 98.44% at 10,000 samples vs 41.41% for vote or reward-model pick; AIMO 3 gpt-oss-120b: best majority vote 42/50 vs pass@20 45.5; 2% to 46% of trajectories that sample the correct answer end with a wrong plurality; PaLM 2-L oracle pick beats self-consistency by about 6 points (GSM8K) and about 20 (MATH). A strict code check closes much of the gap where one exists: SWE-bench Lite 15.9% to 56% with unit tests; an exact multiset filter 74.2% to 92.2% with no new errors.
agent_test: Log, for each solved item, whether the right hypothesis was in the pool; report pool coverage next to final accuracy so selection loss is visible.

claim: On ARC with GPT-4 most of the loss between 'correct hypothesis in the pool' and 'correct program' is implementation, not selection: 49 of 100 tasks had a correct hypothesis, a human choosing it gave 33 correct programs (67%) after 3 rounds of execution feedback, an LLM summary step gave 30, and a likelihood reranker put the correct hypothesis in the top 16 of 64 on only 10 of 21 tasks. One paper, one model.
agent_test: Before building a selector, measure how often a known-correct hypothesis fails at implementation; the held-out gate only helps the selection share (about 3 tasks in 100 here).

claim: Fit to the shown examples is a weak gate; a held-out or differential check is stricter. CodeARC: of o3-mini's first synthesised functions, 67.6% pass the 10 initial examples but 38.9% pass the oracle (28.7 points of false accepts). BARC: about 9% of sampled programs that fit the training examples are false positives, half of which still lose to a majority vote. Test suites also err: 11.3% of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky tests; one deterministic gate in an agent study had 5% precision while another had 100%.
agent_test: Run every candidate rule on cases not shown at fit time; measure each gate's own precision and false-reject rate on known-good and known-bad candidates.

claim: An explanatory bonus gives early false confidence and its best size is small and setting-specific. Trpin and Pellert (bonus 0.1): above 0.95 on a false coin at the first assignment in 47% of runs vs 3% for Jeffrey updating; they did not vary the bonus. Douven (2020), ICU simulation with bonus drawn from 0 to 0.25: surviving agents settle near c = 0.010, EXPL agents die out in large numbers early, and fitness gains are tiny (0.873 vs 0.871 and 0.872). Simulations only, no language model tested.
agent_test: If a bonus is added in S7, keep it near 0.01 on the probability scale, use it only to break near-ties, and forbid acceptance on a bonus alone until a held-out check passes. Test c from 0 to 0.1 on a pool of known answers.

claim: Explaining before predicting pushes LLMs toward the broad rule and slows learning of exceptions, as it does people. Vehicle task, 80% rule plus exceptions: mean rounds to learn all labels direct vs CoT: GPT-4o 2.9 vs 12.5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 2.3 vs 6.4, Claude 3 Opus 2.4 vs 5.5; GPT-4o with CoT stagnated at 80% per round. Human basis: Williams, Lombrozo and Rehder 2013 (abstract only).
agent_test: When the rule explains most but not all cases, keep a separate list of exceptions and test the rule on it; do not let the self-explanation step overwrite the case memory.

claim: What predicts whether hypothesis-then-test helps: it helps when the true rule is short, symbolic and may combine several concepts (ACRE 64.0 to 82.5 raw, List Functions 65.1 to 71.2, ARC induction on composition), and fails when the structure is perceptual or the rule needs a wide context. MiniARC raw 33.1 to 18.7; ConceptARC single-concept perceptual items favour direct prediction; InductionBench compatibility is 0 for all but o3-mini at window size 4 (o3-mini 5.69% overall). No study tested a predictor directly; the pattern is read across three papers.
agent_test: S0 can route by a cheap check: can the rule be written as a short program that runs on the examples? If no candidate fits any example after N tries, switch to direct answering and say so.

claim: The bad-lot gate is untested. No benchmark with candidate pools that lack the true explanation was found. What exists: models rarely say none fit (K08); a code rule 'no candidate fits the data' is the natural gate (Li et al. use 'no hypothesis explains the examples' to switch mode), but a verifier that checks only the observed case accepts trivial local fixes (DeFAb: simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 tasks).
agent_test: Build a small test of pools with the true rule removed (distractors only) and measure how often the gate says none fit; include a transfer set so a local fix cannot pass.

claim: Reasoning effort alone does not fix attribution of interacting causes. Elenchos: GPT-5.4 detection 0.86 vs attribution 0.37; attribution 0.41 at low and 0.47 at medium reasoning; Gemini 2.5 Pro detection 0.93 vs attribution 0.35; earlier files record 0.32 for one change vs 0.03 for interacting changes. In composed causal arithmetic o1 stayed flat across more mediators while other models did not (a different task). Whether a code-built diff table or an impasse step would flatten the curve is untested.
agent_test: Add a code-built 'what changed' table and an impasse step and run on Elenchos with k = 1, 2, 3; compare attribution accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Set-level scores at inference time are untested for abduction. GEAR used consistency, generalisation and diversity for evaluation and as a training signal only. The nearest inference-time evidence is from code: CodeT's execution agreement score (HumanEval 47.0 to 65.8) and the finding that prompt diversity among voters did not raise accuracy (AIMO 3: code-first mean 37.7 vs baseline 39.3).
agent_test: Run best-of-N on a hypothesis pool with three selectors (vote, model judge, code-computed consistency plus held-out fit) at equal tokens.

claim: A code check on the observed case alone rewards local fixes. DeFAb: simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 released tasks because every rule body is a single entity fact, and two of six models succeed on all; prompt style changes success sharply (one model 133/336 vs 336/336). The authors propose a contextual task with entities that must change and entities that must not. Preprint with planned studies not yet run.
agent_test: Give the held-out gate two groups: cases the new rule must cover and cases it must leave alone.

claim: The human simplicity preference is not a general prior. Outside the Lombrozo lab, Lim and Oppenheimer (four studies, n = 286, 201, 523, 253) find a preference for explanations about as complex as the event; Zemla et al. (Reddit corpus, abstract only) find simplicity did not predict quality and complexity was preferred; Johnson, Valenti and Keil (abstract only) find stronger simplicity preference in deterministic and physical systems than in stochastic and social ones. No direct replication or failed replication of the 2007 experiments was found. Related LLM result: in-context learning has a built-in compression pressure in theory (Elmoznino et al.).
agent_test: Make any simplicity term depend on the complexity of the data; count unexplained root assumptions, not all causes.
